You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Make her close her jacket fully
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Is her jacket fully closed?
node.criteria: Assess the jacket’s front closure itself by comparing corresponding visible portions in SOURCE and EDITED. Full achievement requires the front panels to meet along the closure with no visible opening remaining. Count partial fulfillment only where visible evidence shows the panels have moved together toward closure while an opening remains. If the closure or its corresponding portions are obscured or cannot be reliably compared, treat the observation as unresolved rather than inferring no progress or progress.
node.binding: Compare the original jacket on the woman in SOURCE with that same jacket in EDITED. Judge only visible evidence at the jacket closure; a changed pose, drape, or unrelated edit is not evidence of closure progress. If the closure is not sufficiently visible for comparison, use insufficient evidence.
node.endpoint: Her jacket is fully closed, with no visible opening along the closure.
node.necessity: This is the requested change and its complete endpoint.
node.zero_when: The corresponding closure is sufficiently visible to compare, and shows no visible movement of the front panels toward one another relative to SOURCE. Do not assign zero when the closure cannot be reliably assessed.
node.half_when: Visible corresponding portions show the front panels moved together toward closure, but a visible opening remains. If the closure is obscured or indeterminate, leave fulfillment unresolved rather than assigning a partial score.
node.full_when: The jacket’s front panels meet along the visible closure, with no visible opening remaining; the closure is sufficiently visible to establish this endpoint.

node_traces.evidence: The jacket’s front closure is visible in the source, where the panels are apart. In the edited image, the woman is turned and the jacket hangs open; the visible panels have not moved together toward closure, and a large opening remains. The requested closure is not achieved.

response.content: {"text":"The trace gives a confident zero based on the edited jacket hanging open, but the changed pose and drape make the corresponding closure difficult to compare; the images do not clearly establish whether the panels moved toward closure. Tighten the node’s evidence rule so it distinguishes visible lack of progress from an unassessable closure, and requires comparison of corresponding closure portions rather than inferring zero from an open-looking silhouette. Preserve the full-closure endpoint and partial-progress criterion. Treat low confidence or pose variation as reasons to investigate, not as proof of either progress or absence; keep genuinely obscured evidence unresolved. This is a visual-evidence/criterion calibration issue, not a transport or schema failure."}
